dialogue.speaker: Interviewer
dialogue.text: Good morning. Please have a seat. Could you tell me a little about yourself and why you're applying to our master's programme?

dialogue.speaker: Kamila
dialogue.text: Good morning. My name is Kamila Seitkali. I'm a final-year linguistics student at WKU in Uralsk. I've been interested in language acquisition research for about two years, which is why I'm applying to your programme.

dialogue.speaker: Interviewer
dialogue.text: Excellent. Do you know what area of linguistics you'd like to specialise in?

dialogue.speaker: Kamila
dialogue.text: Yes — bilingual language acquisition, particularly in early childhood. I'm interested in how children in multilingual households develop both languages simultaneously.

dialogue.speaker: Interviewer
dialogue.text: Could you tell me about any research experience you have?

dialogue.speaker: Kamila
dialogue.text: I've assisted Professor Aidarov at WKU with a research project on bilingual education in Kazakhstan. We collected data from schools in three different regions.

dialogue.speaker: Interviewer
dialogue.text: Interesting. Do you know whether your data will be published?

dialogue.speaker: Kamila
dialogue.text: It hasn't been published yet, but Professor Aidarov has submitted it to a peer-reviewed journal. We're awaiting the response.

dialogue.speaker: Interviewer
dialogue.text: Could you explain what methods you used in the data collection?

dialogue.speaker: Kamila
dialogue.text: We used a combination of classroom observation and structured interviews with both teachers and parents. I personally conducted twelve of the parent interviews.

dialogue.speaker: Interviewer
dialogue.text: I see. Can you tell me what you see as the main challenge in bilingual education research?

dialogue.speaker: Kamila
dialogue.text: I think it's the difficulty of controlling variables. Every child is different, every household is different, and it's hard to isolate one factor from another.

dialogue.speaker: Interviewer
dialogue.text: Very good. Do you happen to know if any of your work has been presented at a conference?

dialogue.speaker: Kamila
dialogue.text: Not yet — but Professor Aidarov is planning to present our findings at a regional conference in Astana in September.

dialogue.speaker: Interviewer
dialogue.text: Could you tell me what you hope to achieve with a master's degree from our programme?

dialogue.speaker: Kamila
dialogue.text: I'd like to develop more rigorous research methodology skills, publish independently, and eventually contribute to educational policy in Kazakhstan.

questions.text: "Could you tell me a little about yourself?" — This is:
questions.hint: "Could you tell me..." = indirect question. Polite structure embedding the question.

questions.text: "Do you know what area you'd like to specialise in?" — The word order after "what area":
questions.hint: In indirect questions, word order is: subject + verb (not inverted). "...what area YOU'D LIKE to specialise in." ✅

questions.text: "Do you know ___ the data will be published?" (indirect yes/no)
questions.hint: "whether" introduces an indirect yes/no question. "Do you know WHETHER it will be published?" ✅

questions.text: "Could you explain what methods you used?" — Why not "what methods did you use"?
opts: In indirect questions, no inversion: "what methods you used" ✅
questions.correct: In indirect questions, no inversion: "what methods you used" ✅
questions.hint: Indirect questions DON'T invert subject+verb. ✅ "...what methods you USED" (not "what methods DID YOU USE").

questions.text: Which is the correct indirect form of "Where is the library?"
opts: "Do you know where is the library?"
"Do you know where the library is?"
"Do you know where the library be?"
"Where is the library, do you know?"
questions.correct: "Do you know where the library is?"
questions.hint: Indirect: "Do you know WHERE THE LIBRARY IS?" — no inversion (library + is, not is + library).

questions.text: "Can you tell me what time does the lecture start?" is correct.
questions.hint: ✅ "Can you tell me what time THE LECTURE STARTS?" — no inversion in indirect question!

questions.text: Which phrase introduces an indirect question most formally?
questions.hint: "Could you tell me...?" is the most formal/polite. "Could" is more formal than "can". ✅

questions.text: "I'd like to know ___ you decided to apply." (indirect "why" question)
questions.hint: "I'd like to know WHY you decided to apply." — "why" stays at the beginning of the embedded question.
